summary: Wildfire Atlas (https://nasa.xiaowan.tw/) is a public web platform that follows wildfires from the satellite pixel, through the atmosphere, to their impact on agriculture. UNEP (2022) projects that extreme wildfires could increase by up to 50% by 2100, so knowing where fires burn, under what weather, and what they cost matters more each year. Our platform brings together NASA FIRMS hotspots, NASA EONET events, NASA GIBS imagery, VIIRS and MODIS satellite files and ERA5 weather for California, Portugal and Southeast Australia. Users can run our VIIRS U-Net model on a NOAA-20 or NOAA-21 overpass to get fire-pixel clusters and their latitude/longitude bounds. They can also compare monthly fire activity with the 2018–2025 historical median, overlay upper-air wind and humidity on the fire map, and use explainable XGBoost models to test how vapour pressure deficit, soil moisture and wind change the modelled likelihood of fire. For recorded fires, the platform shows the official final perimeter next to estimated direct crop losses for California almonds, grapes and pistachios. A four-episode video series supports learning. Every result shows its source, time basis and limitations, so open Earth observations become evidence that users can trace.

The link includes the research pipeline (fire-occurrence models, crop-loss

estimation), training and inference code for the MODIS / VIIRS

fire-detection model, and Wildfire Atlas website deployment package.


What does it do and how does it work?

Wildfire Atlas (https://nasa.xiaowan.tw/) connects satellite observations, atmospheric conditions and agricultural impact for three study regions: California, Portugal and Southeast Australia. The website has eight workspaces.

Fire detection runs our VIIRS U-Net segmentation model on a paired VIIRS L1B radiance and geolocation scene from NOAA-20 or NOAA-21. The model uses nine input channels and a threshold of 0.20, and its checkpoint records a validation F1 of 0.936. It returns predicted fire-pixel clusters, each with its latitude/longitude range, pixel count and model scores, plus a combined WGS84 envelope that can be downloaded as CSV or GeoJSON. Clusters can be overlaid on ASTER GDEM terrain relief and on ERA5 wind, specific humidity and geopotential height at 850 or 250 hPa, matched to the scene’s UTC hour.

Explore shows the historical archive (2,735 recorded events in the current snapshot) on a 3D globe. It displays MODIS and VIIRS hotspots, the official final perimeter, daily ERA5-Land weather and NASA GIBS true-colour imagery, along with each event’s duration, footprint and estimated direct crop loss. Its Recent observations mode reads the NASA EONET event feed and FIRMS near-real-time hotspots and can send a date and region directly to Fire detection.

Historical event builds a monthly fire-activity calendar for each sensor. It compares each month with its historical same-month median (2018–2025, leaving out the year being compared) and shows seasonal and annual patterns. Users can export an HTML report, a ZIP bundle with charts, CSV and JSON, and daily CSV files.

Atmosphere shows hourly ERA5 pressure-level temperature, wind, vertical motion, humidity and geopotential height on an interactive globe. MODIS imagery finds Terra and Aqua Collection 6.1 overpasses and converts the original HDF files into true-colour and Band 31 brightness-temperature images.

Loss & climate compares annual direct burning losses with a separate wine-grape smoke pathway. It runs first-order warming experiments (+1 °C and +2 °C, with and without drier soils). It also provides an XGBoost sandbox where users adjust VPD, soil moisture and wind anomalies, read TreeSHAP feature contributions and find comparable historical climates. A direct loss calculator applies L = A × D × (Y × P + δ × R), so every assumption stays visible.

Education hosts our four-episode Wildfire Series: California, Portugal, Southeast Australia, and Causes & Prevention. Data & methods documents the workflow, data sources, limitations and connected capabilities.

Behind the interface, VIIRS and MODIS detections are filtered against official perimeters and fire periods. ERA5-Land VPD, topsoil moisture and wind are expressed as anomalies relative to a 1991–2020 climatology, using 7-day and 14-day antecedent windows. Region-specific XGBoost models use climate, terrain, cropland fraction and distance to natural vegetation, with a correction for case-control sampling. To estimate direct crop loss, we compare Sentinel-2 vegetation change with control fields and then apply damage fractions, crop area, yield, price and re-establishment costs.

Benefits
Users can go from a fire pixel to its weather context and its economic consequences in one place, without creating an account. Time (UTC), coordinates (WGS84) and units are always stated. Outputs can be downloaded as CSV, GeoJSON, PNG, HDF, HTML or ZIP for GIS, spreadsheets and reports. Ready-made examples, including California on 26 July 2024 and the 2019 Kincade Fire, let new users start right away.

Intended impact
We want wildfire impacts at the agriculture–wildland interface to be quick to assess and easy to explain. The current catalogue contains 1,258,560 source detections and 163 events with direct-loss outputs, and California direct crop-loss estimates total about USD 6.5 million. Researchers can produce regional analyses that others can trace back to the data. Students and the public can learn through the video series. Agricultural stakeholders can explore exposure and test loss scenarios.

Tools and technologies


Data: NASA FIRMS (VIIRS S-NPP, VIIRS NOAA-20 and MODIS), NASA EONET v3, NASA GIBS, VIIRS L1B files through NASA Earthdata, MODIS Collection 6.1 L1B HDF files, ASTER GDEM, NASA Blue Marble, ERA5 pressure levels from the Copernicus Climate Data Store, ERA5-Land through Google Earth Engine, Sentinel-2, USDA NASS Cropland Data Layer, USDA RMA, county crop reports, UC Davis cost studies, NOAA HMS smoke data, Natural Earth, and fire perimeters from CAL FIRE FRAP, EFFIS, DEECA and NSW NPWS.


Models: a U-Net deep-learning segmentation model for VIIRS fire pixels, and region-specific XGBoost occurrence models explained with TreeSHAP.


Web: an interactive 3D globe built with Globe.GL and Three.js, plus embedded YouTube videos.
